title: Pauri 7, meaning: fame without grace
hookLine: live four ages and be well-known everywhere; without His kindly glance, no one asks after you (Japji 7)

cards: The phone lights up, and there's the count. How many people liked the photo. How many read your post.

Whether anyone noticed the thing you worked so hard on. It's human to want to be seen, and it can sting when you aren't. Now stretch that as far as it goes: well-known everywhere on earth, for age upon age.
Guru Nanak's seventh pauri imagines exactly that, and then asks one quiet question about it.

teach.b: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe.

If your life lasted the four ages, and ten times more; if you were known in all nine regions of the world, and everyone walked along with you; if you kept a good name and won praise and renown across the world: if His kindly glance doesn't fall on you, no one will ask after you.
There's the word from pauri four: nadar, the gracious glance.

teach.h: WITHOUT THE GLANCE, NO ONE ASKS.
teach.b: Everything the world admires, long life, fame, followers, a good reputation, is stacked as high as it can go, then weighed against one glance, and the glance is heavier. Then the pauri gets sharper.

Without that glance, it says, a person is like a worm among worms, and even wrongdoers point fingers at him. Strong words, but not an insult to anyone; a picture of how small fame really is, in the end.
Nanak, the One gives virtue to those who have none, and more virtue to the virtuous. And there's no one, the pauri says, who could give Him any virtue in return. So the whole thing flips.

Fame is something the world hands out and takes back. Nadar is something only the Giver gives, freely, even to people who have nothing to show. The pauri doesn't call praise wicked; being thanked is lovely.
It just says fame isn't it: not the thing that lasts, and not the thing that decides whether anyone asks after you.

how: Sikhs recite the seventh pauri each morning; it is often quoted in talks on humility and on seva done without seeking praise.

o: a crowd that walks along with you
the kindly glance of the One
a good name the world remembers

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: pauri seven says praise is wicked
it says fame isn't what lasts; without the glance, no one asks after you.
the One gives virtue even to those who have none
Nanak, He gives virtue to the virtueless, and more to the virtuous.
someone could give the One a virtue in return
there's no one who could give Him any virtue.

games.q: you've lived four ages and are well-known in all nine regions. what does the pauri say happens without His kindly glance?
games.why: je tis nadar na aavaee, ta vaat na puchhai ke: if the glance doesn't fall on you, no one asks after you.

practice: Think of one place where you want to be praised right now, a post, a project, a family argument you want to be seen winning, and notice it in your body: a small leaning forward, a waiting.
Now let the leaning go, sit back, imagine no one ever finds out how good that thing was, and see what's left; maybe there's still something good in it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Nadar. The kindly glance: without it, even a life well-known for four ages and more means no one asks after you.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: to win praise and renown in the world (Japji, pauri 7).

carryVoice: Your line: fame is not it. The glance is given freely, even to those with nothing to show. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 7
